In a ThreadPoolExecutor, what is the actual difference between corePoolSize and maximumPoolSize?
option1: corePoolSize is how many threads exist at startup; maximumPoolSize is how many can ever exist, full stop
option2: corePoolSize is the number of workers created first and kept around by default; maximumPoolSize is the hard ceiling the pool may grow to, but only once the queue can take no more
option3: corePoolSize handles fast tasks, maximumPoolSize handles slow tasks
option4: There is no real difference - both just mean 'number of threads'
correctOptionExplanation: Core threads are the pool's normal size. Extra threads, up to maximumPoolSize, are a last resort - reached for only when the queue itself has refused a task.

option1: 5, because maximumPoolSize always applies immediately
option2: 2 - poolSize only grows to satisfy work that actually arrives, one worker per task until the core is full
option3: 0, because no thread is created until a task finishes
option4: 1, because only one thread is needed for 2 quick tasks
correctOptionExplanation: poolSize climbed 0 -> 1 -> 2, one new worker per submitted task, and stopped exactly at corePoolSize since 2 tasks needed no more than that.

option1: Yes immediately, since poolSize (2) is still less than maximumPoolSize (5)
option2: No - poolSize is already at corePoolSize, so the task goes into the queue instead of getting a new worker
option3: Yes, because the queue is empty so there is 'room' for a new thread
option4: It depends on which task finishes first
correctOptionExplanation: A new worker is only created while poolSize < corePoolSize. Once the core is full, the executor's next move is always to try the queue, never to jump straight to another worker.

option1: 5 - one worker per task up to maximumPoolSize
option2: 2 - tasks 3, 4 and 5 go into the queue; poolSize does not move at all
option3: 3 - one extra worker is created because the queue would otherwise overflow
option4: It cannot be determined without knowing task duration
correctOptionExplanation: Verified: poolSize stayed at 2 through all five submissions, while queued climbed 0,0,1,2,3. The pool does not react to busy core threads by growing - it reacts by queueing.

option1: Simply having more than corePoolSize tasks submitted
option2: The queue must refuse a task - which only happens once it is completely full
option3: A task must run for longer than 3 seconds
option4: maximumPoolSize must be reached first
correctOptionExplanation: This is the whole ordering rule in one sentence: extra workers exist to handle a task the queue could not accept, not to handle 'busyness' in general.

option1: They wait in the queue behind tasks 3, 4 and 5
option2: The queue is already full (3/3) by the time they arrive, so each one forces a brand new worker to be created for it - poolSize climbs 2->3->4->5
option3: They are rejected, since the queue is full
option4: They replace tasks 3, 4 and 5 in the queue
correctOptionExplanation: Tasks 1-2 get core workers, 3-5 fill the queue, and only then does the executor start creating extra workers - one per task, since the queue has nowhere left to put them.

option1: Tasks 3-5, because they were submitted first
option2: Tasks 6-8, because they started running immediately on new workers, while 3-5 were still sitting in the queue waiting their turn
option3: All 8 finish at the same time
option4: It alternates - 3, 6, 4, 7, 5, 8
correctOptionExplanation: Submission order and execution order are different things. A task queued early can easily finish LATER than a task submitted after it, if that later task got its own worker instead of waiting.

questionText:
Put these four steps in the order ThreadPoolExecutor actually follows when a new task is submitted:

  A. create another worker (up to maximumPoolSize)
  B. reject the task
  C. create a worker (while below corePoolSize)
  D. try to add the task to the queue
option1: A, C, D, B
option2: C, D, A, B
option3: D, C, A, B
option4: C, A, D, B
correctOptionExplanation: corePoolSize first, then the queue, then extra workers up to maximumPoolSize, and only if all three fail is the task rejected. Skipping straight to 'add a worker' the moment core is busy is the single most common misconception.

option1: 20, since every task eventually needs a thread
option2: 6 - maximumPoolSize is a hard ceiling no matter how many tasks are waiting
option3: 4, matching the queue capacity
option4: 2, because the queue will simply absorb everything
correctOptionExplanation: corePoolSize + queue capacity + (maximumPoolSize - corePoolSize) is the total the pool can be actively working on or holding. Nothing pushes poolSize past maximumPoolSize, ever.

option1: It grows steadily from 3 up toward 10
option2: It goes to 3 and never changes again - with core equal to max there is no 'extra worker' tier at all, so the queue (and eventually rejection) does all the remaining work
option3: It stays at 0 until the queue is full
option4: It immediately jumps to 5, matching the queue capacity
correctOptionExplanation: When corePoolSize == maximumPoolSize, step A of the ordering rule (create an extra worker) can never fire, because there is no room above the core. Everything past the first 3 tasks depends entirely on the queue.

option1: It gets a new worker, since maximumPoolSize allows more threads
option2: It is rejected - 3 running + 5 queued = 8 tasks accommodated, and the 9th has nowhere to go since core==max blocks the extra-worker step entirely
option3: It waits indefinitely with no error
option4: It silently overwrites task 8 in the queue
correctOptionExplanation: Total capacity here is corePoolSize (3) + queue capacity (5) = 8. Setting core equal to max is a legitimate way to build a strictly bounded, no-growth pool.

option1: 4, because corePoolSize always creates that many threads upfront
option2: 1 - a core worker is created lazily, only as tasks actually arrive needing one, not all at once when the executor is built
option3: 0, because 1 task is not enough to trigger core creation
option4: It depends on maximumPoolSize
correctOptionExplanation: corePoolSize is a target ceiling for the lazy-creation phase, not a guaranteed headcount from the moment the executor exists. (A separate method, prestartAllCoreThreads(), exists specifically for anyone who wants them created upfront - not used in these experiments.)

option1: Coincidence - the numbers happen to match
option2: In experiment 1 there simply isn't enough work to need more than 2 workers. In experiment 2 there IS more work, but the queue absorbs tasks 3-5 before the executor ever needs to create a third worker
option3: Because both experiments use the same SleepTask class
option4: Because ArrayBlockingQueue always limits poolSize to corePoolSize
correctOptionExplanation: Same ending number, completely different reasons - one from insufficient demand, one from the queue doing its job. Reading poolSize alone never tells you which situation you're in; you have to check queued too.

option1: poolSize=5, queued=1
option2: poolSize=2, queued=3, plus 1 extra worker created for the 6th -> poolSize=3, queued=3
option3: poolSize=6, queued=0
option4: poolSize=2, queued=4
correctOptionExplanation: Tasks 1-2 -> core workers. Tasks 3-5 -> fill the queue (now full at 3). Task 6 finds the queue full, so it forces a new worker: poolSize becomes 3, queued stays at 3.

option1: Always exactly 6
option2: It equals however many tasks have been submitted so far MINUS how many have already completed - it is not a fixed number, it just tracks total accepted work not yet finished
option3: Always exactly corePoolSize + queue capacity
option4: Always exactly maximumPoolSize
correctOptionExplanation: poolSize+queued is 'how much accepted work exists right now', which naturally grows as tasks arrive and shrinks as they finish - there's no fixed target for it to equal.

questionText: A colleague says: 'maximumPoolSize is basically decoration - the pool almost never actually uses the extra threads.' Based on everything in experiments 1-3, is that a fair generalisation?
option1: Yes, extra workers are essentially never created in practice
option2: No - it depends entirely on whether the queue fills up. With a small or full queue, extra workers get created constantly; the real variable is queue behaviour, which the next several experiments dig into
option3: Yes, because maximumPoolSize only matters for SynchronousQueue
option4: No, extra workers are always created immediately regardless of the queue
correctOptionExplanation: This is exactly the pivot for the rest of the quiz: whether maximumPoolSize 'does anything' is entirely a property of the QUEUE, not of maximumPoolSize itself.

option1: 5, matching maximumPoolSize
option2: 8 - maximumPoolSize (5 running) plus queue capacity (3 waiting)
option3: 3, matching the queue capacity only
option4: Unlimited, since AbortPolicy only throws for the queue
correctOptionExplanation: Verified: task 8 was accepted (poolSize=5, queued=3), task 9 threw RejectedExecutionException. Total capacity is always maximumPoolSize + queue capacity for a bounded queue.

option1: The task is large, the JVM is low on memory, and the queue is a LinkedBlockingQueue
option2: poolSize has reached maximumPoolSize, the queue is completely full, and another task is submitted anyway
option3: corePoolSize is 0, the queue is empty, and shutdown() has been called
option4: The task throws an exception when run() executes
correctOptionExplanation: Missing any one of the three means the task gets accepted somewhere - a free worker, a free queue slot, or room to grow the pool. Rejection is specifically what happens when none of those exist.

option1: 8, unchanged
option2: 11 - maximumPoolSize (5) + the new queue capacity (6)
option3: 6, matching only the new queue capacity
option4: 5, matching only maximumPoolSize
correctOptionExplanation: Total capacity always tracks maximumPoolSize + queue capacity for a bounded queue - change either number and the rejection point moves with it.

option1: Nothing is rejected - a default handler always accepts
option2: The exact same thing as AbortPolicy - it IS the default policy when none is given
option3: The task is silently dropped instead of throwing
option4: A NullPointerException occurs because no policy was set
correctOptionExplanation: AbortPolicy isn't just one option among several - it's what you already get if you don't pick anything. Deliberately naming it made the choice visible rather than accidental.

option1: poolSize
option2: active
option3: queued
option4: completed
correctOptionExplanation: completed and everScheduled (getTaskCount()) are running totals since the executor was created. poolSize, active and queued are snapshots of right now and can rise and fall freely as work arrives and finishes.

A worker thread exists, has picked up a task, but the task's run() method has a bug and is stuck in an infinite loop doing nothing useful. What do poolSize and active read for that worker?
option1: poolSize counts it, active does not - a stuck task is not 'active'
option2: Both poolSize and active count it - the executor has no way to know the task is stuck, so as far as it can tell that worker is legitimately busy
option3: Neither counts it, since the task never calls a method the executor tracks
option4: poolSize drops to exclude it once it has run for 'too long'
correctOptionExplanation: active simply means 'currently running something', with no concept of whether that something is making progress. A hung task looks identical to a genuinely busy one from the executor's point of view - this is exactly why timeouts on individual tasks are a separate concern the pool does not solve for you.

option1: active always equals poolSize - they are the same number
option2: active reads 5 here, matching poolSize. But yes, active can be lower: a worker that exists but currently has no task to run (idle, waiting for the next one) counts in poolSize but not in active
option3: active is always 0 unless a task is submitted this exact instant
option4: active can never be measured while tasks are running
correctOptionExplanation: A pool can have, say, poolSize=5 and active=2 once most of the burst work has finished but the extra workers haven't timed out yet - three threads exist and are idle, not gone and not busy.

questionText: A pool reports poolSize=5, active=3, queued=2, completed=40, everScheduled=45. How many tasks does this pool still have left to get through (running plus waiting)?
option4: Both B and C are correct, and they agree by definition
correctOptionExplanation: active (currently running) + queued (currently waiting) is exactly the same quantity as everScheduled minus completed - two different ways of counting the same unfinished work.

questionText: Which pair of counters would you check to find out whether an executor is currently under so much pressure that it has been forced past its normal core size?
option1: completed and everScheduled
option2: poolSize and corePoolSize - if poolSize exceeds corePoolSize, the executor has had to create extra workers, meaning the queue filled up at some point
option3: active and queued added together
option4: There is no way to tell this from the counters
correctOptionExplanation: poolSize above corePoolSize is direct evidence the queue was once full enough to force growth - a genuinely useful health signal for a running system.

option1: Yes, they always mean exactly the same thing
option2: No - active < poolSize means some existing WORKER has nothing to do; queued > 0 means some TASK has nowhere to run yet. A pool can have both, either, or neither at once
option3: No - active < poolSize is impossible, so the question doesn't apply
option4: Yes, because both numbers come from the same underlying field
correctOptionExplanation: Picture a burst that just finished: workers still exist and are momentarily idle (active < poolSize) while the queue is empty (queued = 0). Or the opposite during a growing burst. Two independent signals, not two names for the same thing.

option1: It ran briefly and then was cancelled
option2: It was never run at all and never entered the queue - execute() failed before the task was accepted anywhere
option3: It is queued and will run once space frees up
option4: It ran on the calling thread instead
correctOptionExplanation: Rejection means the task was refused entry entirely. Whatever work it represented simply did not happen, unless the calling code does something about the exception (retry it, log it, run it another way).

option1: No, rejection can only happen once poolSize equals maximumPoolSize
option2: Yes - if the QUEUE were unbounded this could never happen, but if using a bounded queue smaller than expected, or if maximumPoolSize was reached and then a worker died and was replaced slower than tasks arrived, timing edge cases are possible. In the straightforward case shown here though: no, rejection strictly requires poolSize == maximumPoolSize AND the queue full
option3: Yes, rejection is random and can happen at any time
option4: Yes, whenever more than corePoolSize tasks exist
correctOptionExplanation: For the executors built in these experiments, rejection is deterministic: pool at max AND queue full AND a new task arrives. All three, together, every time.

option1: How long a task is allowed to run before being killed
option2: How long an IDLE non-core worker thread is allowed to sit with nothing to do before it is allowed to terminate
option3: How long the whole executor stays alive before shutting down automatically
option4: How long a task can wait in the queue before being discarded
correctOptionExplanation: It has nothing to do with tasks or the queue directly - it is purely about how patient the pool is with a worker that currently has no work.

option1: It stays at 5 forever, since threads never terminate once created
option2: It falls back down to 2 - the 3 extra (non-core) workers time out after about 5 idle seconds each, while the 2 core workers stay alive
option3: It falls all the way to 0
option4: It grows further, since idle time causes more workers to be created
correctOptionExplanation: keepAliveTime by default only applies to threads ABOVE corePoolSize. The 2 core workers are exempt and simply wait for the next task, however long that takes.

option1: It is a bug - they should never have been created
option2: They were needed to handle a genuine burst of demand. Once the burst passes, keeping unused threads around wastes memory and OS resources, so the pool sheds them back down to its normal size
option3: Java requires exactly 5 workers whenever maximumPoolSize is 5
option4: They are created for load-testing purposes only
correctOptionExplanation: This is the entire point of keepAliveTime: let the pool grow to absorb a spike, then shrink back once the spike passes, rather than either permanently over-provisioning or rejecting the spike outright.

option1: Nothing - core threads always eventually time out regardless
option2: It removes the exemption core threads normally have: with it enabled, even the original 2 core workers can time out and disappear if idle for longer than keepAliveTime, so the pool can shrink all the way to 0
option3: It makes non-core threads immune to timing out instead
option4: It only affects threads created after the method is called
correctOptionExplanation: Without this call, corePoolSize is a floor the pool never goes below while idle. With it, there is no floor at all - an idle pool can genuinely go empty.

option1: Experiment 6: 2, Experiment 7: 2 - identical, since keepAliveTime is the same
option2: Experiment 6: 2 (core workers survive), Experiment 7: 0 (core workers also time out)
option3: Experiment 6: 0, Experiment 7: 2 - the opposite
option4: Both reach 0, since 20 seconds is much longer than keepAliveTime either way
correctOptionExplanation: Same keepAliveTime value, completely different floor, purely because of the one boolean flag. This is the cleanest illustration that 'core thread' describes creation priority, not permanence.

questionText: A pool has corePoolSize=0, maximumPoolSize=10, and a bounded queue. Is this a legal, sensible configuration?
option1: No, corePoolSize can never be 0
option2: Yes - it means ALL workers are treated as 'extra' and can time out when idle, so with no work at all the pool can shrink to zero threads, only creating workers as tasks actually arrive
option3: Yes, but the pool will never process any tasks
option4: No, because the queue would then be ignored entirely
correctOptionExplanation: corePoolSize=0 is a legitimate way to build a pool that fully empties out during quiet periods without needing allowCoreThreadTimeOut at all, since there's no core tier to be exempt in the first place.

option1: Because 0 is not a valid long value
option2: Because a keepAliveTime of 0 combined with allowing core threads to time out would mean every idle worker - including brand new core ones - could be torn down virtually instantly, defeating the entire purpose of having a pool of reusable threads
option3: Because keepAliveTime of 0 is reserved for SynchronousQueue only
option4: There is no real restriction - the Javadoc is just a suggestion
correctOptionExplanation: A pool that destroys its own workers the instant they go idle isn't really pooling anything - you'd be back to creating a fresh thread per task, which is exactly what a thread pool exists to avoid.

option1: Yes, it always expires exactly every 5 seconds regardless of activity
option2: No - the idle timer only starts counting once a worker has genuinely nothing left to do. Picking up new work almost immediately resets that clock before it can reach 5 seconds
option3: Yes, because keepAliveTime is measured from when the thread was first created
option4: It depends on which queue implementation is used
correctOptionExplanation: keepAliveTime measures idle time specifically, not total lifetime. A consistently busy extra worker never times out, no matter how long the pool has been running.

option1: 5 seconds is required by the ArrayBlockingQueue class
option2: So the timeout could actually be OBSERVED within a reasonable demo length - with 60 seconds, you would need to wait a full minute of idle time before seeing any change in poolSize
option3: Because allowCoreThreadTimeOut only works with values under 10 seconds
option4: It makes no difference to the demo either way
correctOptionExplanation: The keepAliveTime value in experiments 1-5 was irrelevant to what they were testing, so it was left generous. Experiments 6 and 7 exist specifically to observe this timeout, so it was shortened to make the wait practical.

questionText: Which single sentence best captures what 'core thread' actually means in ThreadPoolExecutor, given experiments 6 and 7?
option1: A thread that is permanently pinned and can never be destroyed under any configuration
option2: A thread the pool prioritises creating first and keeps around by default while idle - but that guarantee can be switched off with allowCoreThreadTimeOut
option3: A thread that runs only the first task ever submitted
option4: A special, faster kind of thread reserved for urgent work
correctOptionExplanation: 'Core' describes a default policy (create these first, keep these around), not an unbreakable property of the thread itself.

What is the practical downside of an unbounded queue that experiment 8's design comment specifically warns about?
option1: Tasks execute out of order
option2: Work piles up in memory instead of being rejected or triggering more workers - under sustained overload, an unbounded queue can grow until the JVM runs out of memory, rather than failing fast
option3: The queue becomes slower to read from as it grows
option4: Tasks time out after 60 seconds automatically

questionText: If you needed a policy that guarantees NO work is ever silently lost, but you also cannot allow the producer thread to be blocked doing someone else's work, which of the four policies (Abort, CallerRuns, Discard, DiscardOldest) fits, and why do the other three fail this requirement?
option1: CallerRunsPolicy - it never loses work and never blocks
option2: AbortPolicy - it loses no work (the caller finds out and can retry/log/handle it), and it never runs the task on the caller's thread. CallerRuns avoids losing work but DOES occupy the caller; Discard and DiscardOldest both silently lose work
option3: DiscardOldest, since only the oldest task is ever affected
option4: None of the four policies satisfy both requirements
correctOptionExplanation: AbortPolicy is the only one that hands the decision back to the caller without making that decision FOR them (by running it, or silently dropping it) - the caller retains full control over what to do next.

questionText: Across all four rejection policies, which single fact stays exactly the same in every one of them?
option1: The task is always eventually run somewhere
option2: The condition that triggers the policy at all - pool at maximumPoolSize AND queue completely full - is identical across all four. Only the RESPONSE to that condition differs
option3: The submitting thread is always blocked
option4: An exception is always thrown
correctOptionExplanation: It's easy to think of the policies as changing WHEN rejection happens. They don't - they only change WHAT HAPPENS once that one specific condition (already established in section 2) is met.

option1: They are discarded immediately, same as new submissions
option2: They are left alone and allowed to run to completion normally - shutdown() only blocks NEW submissions, it does not touch work already accepted
option3: They are moved to a new executor
option4: They throw RejectedExecutionException retroactively
correctOptionExplanation: shutdown() is a polite close: 'stop letting new people in, but let everyone already inside finish their business.'

option4: It runs on the calling thread automatically

questionText: A Future's get() method is declared to throw both InterruptedException and ExecutionException. What real-world situation does EACH of those two correspond to?
option1: Both mean the same thing: the task failed
option2: InterruptedException means the CALLING thread (the one that called get()) was itself interrupted while waiting. ExecutionException means the TASK being waited for threw an exception during its own execution, and that exception is wrapped inside as the cause
option3: InterruptedException means the task was cancelled; ExecutionException means the pool shut down
option4: Neither can actually occur when calling get() with no timeout argument
correctOptionExplanation: Two completely different failures living in the same method signature: one is about YOU (the waiter) being interrupted, the other is about the WORK ITSELF having gone wrong.

option1: submit() is always slower, so execute() is preferred for performance-critical code
option2: If nobody needs to track, wait for, or cancel that specific task, execute() communicates that intent more simply - and avoids creating a Future object that will never be inspected, which is a small but real bit of unnecessary bookkeeping
option3: execute() is required for any Runnable that doesn't implement Callable
option4: There is no legitimate reason - submit() should always be preferred
correctOptionExplanation: Not every piece of code needs every capability. Choosing the simpler method when you genuinely don't need the extra one is a reasonable, deliberate choice, not a missed opportunity.

option1: They are the same operation, named differently for convenience
option2: get() waits for the task to finish and hands you its result; cancel() attempts to stop the task from finishing at all, by interrupting it if it's already running
option3: get() stops the task; cancel() waits for it
option4: get() only works on Callables; cancel() only works on Runnables

option1: No, a Future must be interacted with for the task to actually execute
option2: Yes - the task was already handed to the pool the moment submit() was called; the Future is only a handle for OBSERVING or CONTROLLING it afterward, not a trigger for whether it runs at all

questionText: A single ThreadPoolExecutor is configured with corePoolSize=4, maximumPoolSize=4, and an unbounded queue - a common shape for a general-purpose background pool. questionText: In one sentence each, state what changes and what stays the same about ThreadPoolExecutor's core ordering rule (core -> queue -> extra workers -> reject) regardless of which BlockingQueue implementation is plugged in.
option1: The ordering rule itself changes completely depending on the queue class used
option2: The ordering rule NEVER changes - it is always core, then queue, then extra workers, then reject. What changes between queue implementations is only WHETHER and WHEN step 2 (the queue) actually succeeds or refuses a task, which in turn changes how often steps 3 and 4 get reached
option3: Only SynchronousQueue follows this rule; all other queues skip straight to rejection
option4: The rule applies only to ArrayBlockingQueue
correctOptionExplanation: The single most important idea to leave this quiz with, stated directly: one fixed algorithm, four queue implementations that each answer step 2 differently, and that single difference is what produces every distinct behaviour seen across sections 4 through 8.
